summary: Defines an IMAP extension letting a client use the result of the last SEARCH as input to a later command, without the server sending the message list back to the client first. This saves round trips and lets commands be pipelined. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary:
When an email client searches a mailbox, it usually wants to act on the messages it found, such as fetching or deleting them. This extension lets the server hold on to the search result, so the client can refer to it with a single character instead of sending the whole list of message numbers back.

The client asks for the result to be saved, then uses the $ marker where a list of messages would normally go. The two commands can also be sent together, without waiting for the first reply.

subtitle: Lets an IMAP client reuse the result of a SEARCH as the input to the next command, without sending the message list back to the server.

tldr.problem: IMAP clients often search a mailbox and then act on the messages they found. Doing that with standard commands means the server sends the whole message list back, the client parses it, reformats it and sends it back again, and the two commands cannot be pipelined.
tldr.mechanism: A SEARCH command can carry a new result option, SAVE, which tells the server to remember the list of messages it found in an internal variable. A later command can then use the marker $ in place of a message sequence or UID sequence, and the server substitutes the remembered list.
tldr.outcome: The client saves bandwidth and a round trip, can pipeline the two commands, and the server can apply its own optimisations. A server that advertises SEARCHRES must also implement the ESEARCH extension, and it may refuse to save a result, answering with the NOTSAVED response code.

today: RFC 5182 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 3501 and defines the SEARCHRES capability that an IMAP4 server advertises in its CAPABILITY response.

sections.title: Why Reuse the Search Result
sections.content:
Many IMAP clients use the result of a SEARCH command as the input to another operation, for example fetching the found messages, deleting them, or copying them to another mailbox. This can be done with the standard operations described in RFC 3501, but it is suboptimal. The server sends the list of found messages to the client, and the client then has to parse that list, reformat it and send it back to the server.

Two costs follow. The client cannot pipeline the SEARCH command with the following command, so the round trip is not avoided. And the server might not be able to perform some optimisations, because it can no longer see which messages the two commands have in common.

The extension defines a new SEARCH result option, SAVE, which tells the server to remember the result of the SEARCH or UID SEARCH command, as well as of any command based on SEARCH such as SORT and THREAD, and to store it in an internal variable that this document calls the search result variable. The client can then use the $ marker to reference the content of that variable.

The marker can be used instead of a message sequence or a UID sequence, to indicate that the server should substitute the list of messages from the search result variable. The document lists four advantages: it avoids wasted bandwidth and associated delay; it allows the client to pipeline a SEARCH command with a subsequent FETCH, STORE, COPY, SEARCH or UID EXPUNGE command; the client does not spend time reformatting the result of a SEARCH command into a message set; and it allows the server to perform optimisations, for example deciding which pipelined commands may or may not be executed out of order.

In the absence of any other SEARCH result option, the SAVE result option also suppresses any SEARCH response that would otherwise be returned by the SEARCH command.
sections.plainLanguage:
When an email client searches a mailbox, it usually wants to act on the messages it found, such as fetching or deleting them. This extension lets the server hold on to the search result, so the client can refer to it with a single character instead of sending the whole list of message numbers back.

The client asks for the result to be saved, then uses the $ marker where a list of messages would normally go. The two commands can also be sent together, without waiting for the first reply.

sections.title: The Search Result Variable
sections.content:
The extension is present in any IMAP4 server implementation that returns SEARCHRES as one of the supported capabilities in the CAPABILITY command response. Any such server MUST also implement the ESEARCH extension defined in RFC 4731.

The variable is reset in defined situations. Upon successful completion of a SELECT or an EXAMINE command, after the tagged OK response, the current search result variable is reset to the empty sequence. If the server decides to send a new UIDVALIDITY value while the mailbox is opened, that also causes the search variable to be reset to the empty list.

A successful SEARCH command with the SAVE result option sets the value of the search result variable to the list of messages found in the SEARCH command. If no messages were found, the variable holds the empty list. Three kinds of SEARCH command MUST NOT change the variable: a SEARCH command that caused the server to return the BAD tagged response, a SEARCH command with no SAVE result option that caused the server to return a NO tagged response, and a successful SEARCH command with no SAVE result option. A SEARCH command with the SAVE result option that caused the server to return a NO tagged response sets the variable to the empty sequence.

Two further rules keep the list accurate. When a message listed in the search result variable is expunged, it is automatically removed from the list. If the server stores the list as a list of message numbers, it MUST adjust those numbers automatically when notifying the client about expunged messages. And even when the $ marker holds the empty list of messages, every command that accepts a message set must treat it as a valid but non-matching list: a FETCH $ command returns a tagged OK response and no FETCH responses.

Implementors are reminded that $ can reference IMAP message sequences or UID sequences, depending on the context. A $ set by a SEARCH (SAVE) command can be used as a parameter to a UID FETCH command, which accepts a UID sequence, and a $ set by a UID SEARCH (SAVE) command can be used as a parameter to a FETCH command, which accepts a message sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: The server keeps one list of messages: the result of the last search it was asked to save. The list is emptied when the client opens a mailbox, and a message that is deleted is dropped from it as well. If the list is empty, commands that use it still work, they simply match nothing.

sections.title: Example Exchanges
sections.content:
The first example fetches the headers of the messages found by a search. The client sends A282 SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) FLAGGED SINCE 1-Feb-1994 NOT FROM "Smith" and the server answers A282 OK SEARCH completed, result saved. The client then sends A283 FETCH $ (UID INTERNALDATE FLAGS RFC822.HEADER) and the server returns the three matching messages, with the message numbers 2, 84 and 882.

The second example shows the same two commands pipelined. The client sends the SEARCH and the FETCH back to back without waiting, and the server replies to the SEARCH first and then to the FETCH.

The third example feeds one search into another. After a SEARCH that saved its result, the client sends A301 UID SEARCH UID $ SMALLER 4096, which restricts the second search to the messages the first one found. The client could equally have written A301 UID SEARCH $ SMALLER 4096, and the result would be the same.

The fourth example shows that $ can be combined with other message numbers using the OR search criterion, as in P283 SEARCH CHARSET UTF-8 (OR $ 1,3000:3021) TEXT {8}.

The fifth example shows what a failed search does. When the charset is not supported, the server answers B283 NO [BADCHARSET UTF-8] KOI8-R is not supported, and the saved result variable then contains no messages. A client that wants to retry with another charset has to repeat the earlier search as well, unless it included the charset in the earliest search of the sequence.

The sixth example shows that using $ when it contains no messages is not an error: a COPY command that matches nothing still returns a tagged OK response.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same pattern in several forms. One client searches and saves the result, then fetches the headers of the messages that were found. Another sends the search and the fetch together. A third feeds a search result into a second search, so the second search only looks at the messages the first one found.

sections.title: Several Commands in Progress
sections.content:
Use of a SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) command followed by a command using the $ marker creates a direct dependency between the two commands. As directed by Section 5.5 of RFC 3501, a server MUST execute the two commands in the order they were received. A server capable of out-of-order execution can in some cases execute the two commands in parallel: for example, if a SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) is followed by SEARCH $, the search criteria from the first command can be directly substituted into the second command.

A client supporting this extension MAY pipeline a SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) command with one or more commands using the $ marker, as long as this does not create an ambiguity, as described in Section 5.5 of RFC 3501.

Not every pair of commands is dependent. In one example the client pipelines F282 SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) KEYWORD $Junk with F283 COPY $ "Junk" and F284 STORE $ +FLAGS.Silent (\Deleted), and the three commands run in the order they were sent. In another example the client pipelines a SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) with a second, unrelated SEARCH, and the comment in the example notes that the server can execute the two SEARCH commands in any order, as they have no dependency.

The result of the second SEARCH always overrides the result of the first, so a client that pipelines two saving searches must use the second one.
sections.plainLanguage: A command that uses the saved result depends on the search that saved it, so the server has to run them in the order they arrived. A client may still send both at once. Commands that do not use the saved result have no such dependency, and the server is free to run them in any order.

sections.title: Interaction with the ESEARCH Extension
sections.content:
Servers that implement this extension MUST implement RFC 4731 and conform to the additional requirements in this section. The SAVE result option does not change whether the server would return items corresponding to MIN, MAX, ALL or COUNT.

The value of the $ marker depends on which other result options are present. When SAVE is combined with MIN or MAX, and none of the other ESEARCH result options are present, the corresponding MIN or MAX is returned if the search result is not empty, and the $ marker contains a single message, the one returned in the MIN or MAX return item. When SAVE is combined with both MIN and MAX result options, and no other ESEARCH result options are present, the $ marker contains one or two messages, as returned in the MIN and MAX return items.

When SAVE is combined with the ALL and/or COUNT result options, the $ marker always contains all the messages found by the SEARCH or UID SEARCH command. The document notes that this last rule might affect ESEARCH implementations that optimise how the COUNT result is constructed.
sections.plainLanguage: The saved list does not always hold everything the search found. If the client also asked for only the first or the last match, the saved list holds just that one message. If the client asked for all the matches or for the count, the saved list holds every match.

sections.title: Refusing to Save Search Results
sections.content:
In some cases the server MAY refuse to save a SEARCH (SAVE) result, for example if an internal limit on the number of saved results has been reached. In that case the server MUST return a tagged NO response containing the NOTSAVED response code, and it MUST set the search result variable to the empty sequence, as described in Section 2.1.

The same response is used when a limit on the total number of saved searches across all connections is exceeded, as the security considerations of this document describe.
sections.plainLanguage: The server is allowed to say no. If it has reached a limit on how many search results it will hold, it answers with a failure that includes the code NOTSAVED and empties the saved list.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax specification uses the Augmented Backus-Naur Form, ABNF, as specified in RFC 5234. Non-terminals referenced but not defined below are as defined in RFC 3501 or in RFC 4466.

Except as noted otherwise, all alphabetic characters are case-insensitive. The use of upper- or lower-case characters to define token strings is for editorial clarity only, and implementations MUST accept these strings in a case-insensitive fashion.

The extension adds four productions: the capability production gains the alternative "SEARCHRES"; the sequence-set production gains the alternative seq-last-command, which is the single character $"; the search-return-opt production gains the value "SAVE"; and the resp-text-code production gains the alternative "NOTSAVED".
sections.plainLanguage: The grammar changes are small. A server can list SEARCHRES among its capabilities, a message set can contain the $ character, a search can ask for the SAVE option, and a failure response can carry the code NOTSAVED.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This extension requires the server to keep additional state, and that state may be used to simplify Denial of Service attacks. To limit the damage from such attacks, server implementations MAY limit the number of saved searches they allow across all connections at any given time, and return the tagged NO response containing the NOTSAVED response code to a SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) command when this limit is exceeded.

Apart from that, it is believed that this extension does not raise any additional security concerns beyond those already discussed in RFC 3501.
sections.plainLanguage: Holding on to search results costs the server some memory, and an attacker might use that to help a denial of service attack. A server can therefore cap how many saved searches it keeps at once and refuse the rest.

messages.label: SEARCH RETURN (SAVE)
messages.note: The server stores the list of matching messages.

messages.label: OK SEARCH completed
messages.note: No list of messages is returned.

messages.label: FETCH $
messages.note: The $ marker stands in for the stored list.

messages.label: FETCH RESPONSES
messages.note: The server substitutes the stored list and returns the data.

C: F282 SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) KEYWORD $Junk
C: F283 COPY $ "Junk"
C: F284 STORE $ +FLAGS.Silent (\Deleted)

S: F283 OK COPY completed
S: F284 OK STORE completed
